lines.source: old lab film, line 0: fast on average, can one late response break the budget; transport delay ceiling (150 ms at Level C/D) against a blink of roughly 100 to 400 ms. Thesis stated first.
lines.text: In a flight simulator, a late answer is a wrong answer. It has to answer its pilot within a blink, every single time. Not on average.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 1 and 3: transport delay runs from a primary flight control input to the motion, visual or instrument response (FAA Part 60, EASA CS-FSTD(A)); a device over the limit does not qualify
lines.text: When the pilot moves the controls, the view and the cabin must follow within that blink. It is written into the rules: a simulator that misses it cannot be used to train pilots.

lines.source: old lab film, line 2: every stage spends the budget, image generation the largest share; the stages are the generic chain of a full-flight simulator
lines.text: In that blink, the signal crosses a chain of computers. One reads the controls. One works out how the aircraft flies. One runs its systems. One draws the world. The last updates the screen and moves the cabin.

lines.source: old lab film, line 4: EASA CS-FSTD Issue 1 (ED Decision 2026/008/R, p. 467) sets 100 ms at fidelity level S for new devices
lines.text: Europe's newest standard makes that blink shorter for the most realistic new simulators. The same chain no longer makes it.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 5 to 8: a fixed cadence (60 Hz), hour-long sessions; a four-hour session at 60 Hz is 864,000 frames and one in a thousand is 864 stutters; a deadline is never met on average
lines.text: And not once, but sixty times a second, for hours. Lay out one training session, frame by frame. Even one slip in a thousand comes back hundreds of times, and every one is a jolt the pilot can feel.

lines.source: old lab film, line 9: real overruns cluster, so independence is the optimistic case
lines.text: Worse, the slips bunch together, so the pilot feels a stutter, not a blip.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 10 and 11: a rack of hosts publishes into one frame, which ends when the last host reports
lines.text: Why do frames slip? The work is split across a rack of computers, and every frame has to wait for the slowest one.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 13 and 14: one straggler makes the frame late; budgets are allocated and enforced per host, a system average constrains nobody
lines.text: One slow computer, and the whole frame is late. An average hides it. So every computer gets its own time budget, checked every frame.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 15 to 17: instrument while the session runs; the overrun counter catches what sampled step time misses
lines.text: And every overrun is counted while the simulator runs. Spot checks miss a short spike. A counter does not.

lines.source: old lab film, line 18 (closing line, in plainer words); the series link to the deadline film
lines.text: That is determinism: the slowest frame counts, not the average. It is the rule any AI added to this loop must keep, and the next film shows how.
